notes.meaning: Joab noticed that King David still loved Absalom and missed him deeply. Even though David missed his son, his duty as judge kept him from bringing back a murderer without a good reason. Joab wanted to help David find a way to recall him.

Joab sent to the town of Tekoa for a clever woman who could handle a delicate task. He told her to dress in mourning clothes and skip scented oil, looking like someone who had been grieving for a long time.
Joab gave the woman the exact story she was supposed to tell the king. He planned to use a parable to guide David to a decision before David realized what was happening.

The woman came before David, bowed low to the ground to show great honor to the king, and begged him for help. In Israel, ordinary people could bring difficult legal troubles directly to the king for justice.

David asked what was wrong, and the woman claimed she was a poor, helpless widow whose husband was long dead. This made her situation sound especially heartbreaking and worthy of the king's special protection.

She told the king that her two sons had fought in an open field with no one there to stop them, and one had killed the other. By describing a sudden fight without witnesses, she made the crime sound like an accident rather than a planned murder.

She claimed the whole family demanded the surviving son so they could execute him for his brother's death. She argued this would put out her last glowing coal, wiping out her husband's family name and leaving her with nothing.
David told the woman to go home in peace, promising that he would give orders to protect her. He believed her story and meant to shield her son from the angry relatives.

The woman answered that if sparing her son broke God's law against murder, let any guilt fall on her and her family rather than on David's throne. She said this to press the king to make an immediate, firm ruling.
David assured her that if anyone threatened her or demanded her son, she should bring that person to him. He promised that no one would be allowed to bother her again.

The woman urged David to make a promise in the Lord's name so the family avengers would not destroy her son. David bound himself with an oath, swearing by the living Lord that not a hair of her son's head would fall.
Having secured David's solemn promise to spare a brother's killer, the woman asked permission to speak one more word. David told her to go ahead, not yet realizing the trap she had laid for him.

The woman asked why David did not treat his own son the same way, warning that keeping Absalom in exile hurt God's people. She showed David that by sparing her imaginary son, he had judged himself for keeping his own son away.

She argued that all people must die anyway, disappearing like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered back up. She added that God provides ways to restore those who are cut off rather than simply destroying them.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Catholic Douay-Rheims translation reads this phrase as God not wanting any soul to perish, but desiring that the person cast off be brought back.

notes.meaning: The woman explained that she came to the king because her relatives had frightened her with their demands. She claimed she came hoping that the king's mercy would save her home and family.

She said she trusted the king to rescue her and her son from anyone trying to cut them off from God's land. Her words reminded David that exile separates people from God's heritage and the community of worship.

She praised the king, saying his final ruling would bring true peace because he had wisdom like an angel of God to tell right from wrong. She offered this high praise to lead David toward showing mercy.
David realized that this clever appeal had been planned by someone else and told the woman not to hide the truth from him. She readily agreed to answer whatever he asked.
David asked her plainly whether Joab was behind the whole plan. The woman confessed that David was completely right, admitting that Joab had instructed her and put the exact words into her mouth.
She admitted Joab had arranged the parable to change how David handled Absalom's situation. She praised David again, saying he had wisdom like an angel to know everything happening in his land.

David turned to Joab and granted the request, telling him to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem. Even though David agreed to end the exile, he was not yet ready to welcome Absalom back into his personal fellowship.
Joab bowed low to the ground and blessed the king, thrilled that David had granted his wish. He felt confident that he had won the king's favor and secured good standing with the heir to the throne.
Joab traveled north to Geshur, where Absalom had been living in refuge with his royal grandfather. He brought Absalom safely back to the city of Jerusalem.

David ordered that Absalom must stay in his own home and never enter the royal presence. David gave only half-forgiveness, wanting to show that he still hated the murder while failing to heal the family rift.

Absalom was famous throughout Israel for his handsome looks and had no bodily flaw from head to foot. His outward perfection won the admiration of the people, even though his heart was proud and unrepentant.
Absalom only cut his thick hair when it became too heavy, weighing about two hundred royal shekels after it was cut. His glorious hair fed his vanity, but it would later contribute to his death.

Absalom had three sons and one beautiful daughter, whom he named Tamar after his mistreated sister. The sons are not named and likely died while still young, since Absalom later built a monument because he had no surviving son.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern critical scholars consider the mention of three sons here to contradict a later chapter where Absalom says he has no son to preserve his name.

notes.meaning: Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without ever seeing his father's face. Being kept away from the royal court made him bitter and restless instead of leading him to repent.

Absalom sent for Joab twice so Joab could ask the king to see him, but Joab refused to come. Joab had already secured Absalom's return and did not want to risk losing David's favor by pushing too hard.

Absalom told his servants to set fire to Joab's nearby field of ripe barley to force Joab to pay attention to him. This violent action showed that Absalom was arrogant, reckless, and willing to hurt anyone to get what he wanted.
Joab hurried to Absalom's house and demanded to know why Absalom's servants had burned his field. Joab came to complain, which was exactly what Absalom wanted.

Absalom told Joab that being stuck in Jerusalem was worse than remaining an exile in Geshur. He demanded to see the king face to face, boldly claiming that if he was guilty of any crime, David should execute him.

Joab delivered the message to David, and the king finally summoned Absalom to court. Absalom bowed low to the ground in formal honor, and David kissed him in a gesture of reconciliation, though Absalom showed no true repentance.
